Explaining graph neural network predictions

Source: vignettes/explainability.Rmd
explainability.Rmd
library(graphlearnR)
library(torch)

An explanation answers: which node features and which edges made the model predict this? graphlearnR implements gradient based, perturbation based, and optimization based methods, plus two checks of explanation quality. All methods take a trained graph_fit (or a model), a graph, and a target node; leave target = NULL for a graph level model.

A model to explain 

g <- split_nodes(dataset_karate(), seed = 1)
torch_manual_seed(1)
fit <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("gcn", 34, 16, 2, dropout = 0), g,
                         "node_classification", epochs = 100, seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit, g)
#>              metric     value
#> 1          accuracy 0.8333333
#> 2 balanced_accuracy 0.8333333
#> 3   precision_macro 0.8750000
#> 4      recall_macro 0.8333333
#> 5          f1_macro 0.8285714
#> 6               ece 0.1659179
#> 7             brier 0.3303945
#> 8           roc_auc 1.0000000
#> 9 average_precision 1.0000000

Feature attributions

Saliency

The gradient of the selected output with respect to the input features. By default the output is the predicted class of the target node.

sal <- explain_saliency(fit, g, target = 1)
sal
#> <graph_explanation> saliency for node 1, output 1
top <- order(-abs(sal$node_feature))[1:5]
arrayInd(top, dim(sal$node_feature))
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1   13
#> [2,]    1   33
#> [3,]    1   14
#> [4,]    1    7
#> [5,]    1    4

With identity features, feature j of node i is “being node i”, so the largest saliencies point at the nodes whose identity most affects node 1’s prediction.

Integrated gradients

Saliency is local. Integrated gradients (Sundararajan, Taly, and Yan 2017) average gradients along the straight path from a baseline (zero by default) to the input and multiply by the difference. The attributions then add up to the change in output between baseline and input; graphlearnR reports the remaining gap of the Riemann approximation.

ig <- explain_integrated_gradients(fit, g, target = 1, steps = 64)
sum(ig$node_feature)
#> [1] 9.833233
ig$completeness_gap
#> [1] 0.006706059

Edge attributions

Edge gradients

explain_edges() attaches a weight of one to every edge, takes the gradient of the output with respect to those weights, and returns a table.

eg <- explain_edges(fit, g, target = 1)
head(eg$edges[order(-abs(eg$edges$attribution)), ])
#>    edge from to attribution
#> 32   32   32  1  -0.6392071
#> 22   22   13  1   0.6088946
#> 20   20   12  1   0.5910739
#> 12   12    7  1   0.4951163
#> 10   10    6  1   0.4866577
#> 8     8    5  1   0.4837200

Occlusion

explain_occlusion() removes each incoming edge of the target in turn and records how much the output drops. It also masks each feature column. It is slow for many edges but needs no gradients and is easy to interpret.

oc <- explain_occlusion(fit, g, target = 1)
head(oc$edges[order(-oc$edges$attribution), ])
#>    edge from to attribution
#> 11   22   13  1   0.6274004
#> 10   20   12  1   0.6089334
#> 6    12    7  1   0.5063639
#> 5    10    6  1   0.4981394
#> 4     8    5  1   0.4943419
#> 9    18   11  1   0.4860201

GNNExplainer

gnn_explainer() (Ying et al. 2019) learns a soft mask over edges and features that keeps the prediction while staying small and close to binary. The trained model’s weights are frozen during the optimization and restored afterwards.

gx <- gnn_explainer(fit, g, target = 1, epochs = 100, seed = 1)
head(gx$edges[order(-gx$edges$attribution), ])
#>     edge from to attribution
#> 121  121   24 34   0.9116459
#> 45    45    2 22   0.9104612
#> 56    56   29  3   0.9084590
#> 96    96   34 15   0.9083152
#> 33    33    2  3   0.9076678
#> 124  124   30 24   0.9075592
range(gx$edges$attribution)
#> [1] 0.3414106 0.9116459

Explanation subgraphs

explanation_subgraph() turns any edge attribution into a small graph: the k most important edges (both directions of an undirected pair count as one), the nodes they touch, and the target. Its node_ids map back to the original graph, so it can be plotted or passed to the model again.

sub <- explanation_subgraph(g, gx, k = 5)
sub
#> <graph_data> undirected graph: 8 nodes, 10 edges (5 undirected pairs)
#>   node features [8 x 34]
#>   node labels: factor with 2 levels
#>   masks: train=6, val=0, test=2
sub$node_ids
#> [1]  1  2  3 15 22 24 29 34

Attention

For attention models, attention_weights() collects the coefficients of the last forward pass of each attention layer. Attention is a model component, not an explanation; high attention does not have to mean high influence.

torch_manual_seed(2)
fit_gat <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("gat", 34, 8, 2, heads = 2), g,
                             "node_classification", epochs = 50, seed = 1)
invisible(predict(fit_gat, g))
aw <- attention_weights(fit_gat)
length(aw)
#> [1] 2
head(aw[[1]])
#>   from to      head1      head2
#> 1    1  2 0.19154441 0.16146892
#> 2    2  1 0.03586031 0.07413401
#> 3    1  3 0.16340747 0.13701235
#> 4    3  1 0.05869362 0.03081637
#> 5    1  4 0.22324155 0.21166605
#> 6    4  1 0.12893744 0.06319855

Is the explanation any good?

Fidelity

explanation_fidelity() keeps or removes the k most important edges and measures the change in the predicted probability (Yuan et al. 2022). fidelity_plus is the drop when the important edges are removed (higher is better); fidelity_minus is the drop when only they are kept (lower is better).

rbind(gradient = explanation_fidelity(fit, g, eg, k = 5),
      gnn_explainer = explanation_fidelity(fit, g, gx, k = 5))
#>               fidelity_plus fidelity_minus
#> gradient          1.7281389      -3.426291
#> gnn_explainer    -0.3032961       3.899852

Stability

explanation_stability() perturbs the features with small noise, explains again, and reports the rank correlation with the original explanation. A low value means the explanation would change for inputs that are practically the same.

explanation_stability(fit, g, function(m, h) explain_edges(m, h, target = 1),
                      noise = 0.01, reps = 3, seed = 1)
#> mean_spearman  min_spearman 
#>     0.9977885     0.9963462

Caveats

  • Gradient methods explain the model, not the data. Two models with the same accuracy can have very different explanations.
  • With one hot identity features, feature attributions are about node identity; with real features, they are about feature values.
  • Always check fidelity before you interpret an explanation, and compare against a random edge ranking.
